Suggested mission tasks: Impact geology, ejecta mapping, sample collection practice
Strong matches: Rayed ejecta, normally seen only on airless or thin-atmosphere bodies; iron meteorite impactor
Where it breaks: Sandstone target, not lunar regolith; one small crater; Earth air
Key facts: 45 m wide; under 5,000 years old; found on Google Earth imagery in 2008; 5,178 iron meteorite pieces (about 1.71 tons) recovered
Geology and minerals: Cretaceous sandstone target; ungrouped iron meteorite

Suggested mission tasks: Rover driving over yardangs; sand abrasion tests
Strong matches: Yardangs, crescent dune trains and wind streaks like those seen from Mars orbit; core of the largest hyperarid region on Earth
Where it breaks: Hot, not cold; Earth air pressure
Key facts: USGS and Smithsonian field studies in 1978 to 1984 compared its landforms with Mars; little since. About 200 km west of the Nile
Geology and minerals: Yardangs carved in limestone, Nubian sandstone and old lake sediments
Sources: El-Baz et al. 1979 (https://www.usgs.gov/publications/eolian-features-western-desert-egypt-and-some-applications-mars); Breed et al. 1984 (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19840015443)

Suggested mission tasks: Thermal stress tests of hardware; rover driving on yardangs
Strong matches: Hottest land surface measured from orbit; huge daily temperature swing; large yardang fields
Where it breaks: Hot extreme, while Mars and the lunar poles are cold; thick air
Key facts: MODIS recorded 80.8 °C surface (2002 to 2019 study); daily swing up to about 71 °C; dunes up to 470 m tall
Geology and minerals: Salt desert; dark sand blackened by volcanic lava
Sources: NASA Earth Observatory (https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/irans-lut-desert-153634); Azarderakhsh et al. 2020 (https://modarch.gsfc.nasa.gov/sci_team/pubs/abstract_new.php?id=38105); UNESCO summary (https://c2c.wii.gov.in/lut-desert)

Analog for: Mars (Gale crater and Medusae Fossae yardangs; salt playas)
Suggested mission tasks: Rover tests; instrument tests on salts and clays; biosignature search
Strong matches: Highest desert on Earth: cold, dry, high UV; salt playas; yardangs and polygons similar to those on Mars
Where it breaks: Still has air, liquid water and life
Key facts: Yardang fields cover tens of thousands of sq km (counts range 20,000 to 38,800); evaporation 2,590 mm/yr. Coordinates are a published yardang sample site
Geology and minerals: Lake sediments, salts, chlorite and illite clays, carbonate nodules

Suggested mission tasks: Dust mitigation; dust storm forecasting; wind and abrasion tests
Strong matches: Largest single dust source on Earth; wind lifts dust from a dry lake bed
Where it breaks: Dust is diatomite from an old lake; Earth air is far denser
Key facts: Produces roughly half the dust leaving the Sahara; dust lifts on about 65% of days; part of Lake Megachad about 7,000 years ago
Sources: Washington et al. 2009 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2791565); NASA Earth Observatory (https://science.nasa.gov/?p=1066952)

Site: Harrat Khaybar and Umm Jirsan lava tube, Saudi Arabia
Analog for: Moon and Mars (lava tube shelters); Moon (basalt)
Suggested mission tasks: Habitat-in-cave tests; underground navigation; radar detection of tubes
Strong matches: Large basalt volcanic field with a long lava tube that preserved artifacts for thousands of years
Where it breaks: Lunar tubes may be up to about 1 km wide, far larger; Earth gravity
Key facts: Umm Jirsan: 1,481 m long, about 45 m wide, ceilings up to about 12 m. Field 12,000 to 14,000 sq km; last eruption about 650 CE. Coordinates are the volcanic field's
Sources: Stewart et al. 2024 (Live Science) (https://www.livescience.com/archaeology/humans-were-living-in-a-lava-tube-7000-years-ago-on-the-arabian-peninsula); EarthDate (https://earthdate.org/node/1161); NASA Earth Observatory (https://www.earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/152839/white-and-black-volcanoes-of-saudi-arabia)

Analog for: Mars and Moon (small craters in basalt)
Suggested mission tasks: Impact geology in basalt; sampling; ejecta studies
Strong matches: One of very few craters formed in basalt; target rock similar to Martian basaltic meteorites; ejecta like Martian fluidized ejecta
Where it breaks: Has a lake and vegetation; monsoon climate; Earth air
Key facts: 1.88 km wide; about 37,500 years old by one dating method (others differ); hydrothermal clays formed after impact
Geology and minerals: Deccan Traps basalt; saponite, celadonite, carbonate

Analog for: Mars (salts, acid brines, limits of life)
Strong matches: Polyextreme hot, hypersaline, hyperacidic brines (pH down to -1.7); some pools have no life despite liquid water
Where it breaks: Far hotter and wetter than Mars; active volcanism
Key facts: Dallol dome is 48 m below sea level; the surrounding Danakil Depression floor is about 120 m below. Mean annual air temp about 35 °C. Hot-spring fluids reach 108 °C (water, not ground)
Geology and minerals: Evaporites (halite and other salts), iron minerals
Sources: Kotopoulou et al. 2019 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6380227); Cavalazzi et al. 2019 (phys.org) (https://phys.org/news/2019-05-ultra-small-microbes-extreme-survival-skills.pdf)

Strong matches: Acidic (mean pH 2.3), iron-rich river depositing jarosite and iron oxides like those Opportunity found at Meridiani
Where it breaks: Wet Mediterranean climate; vegetation; Earth air
Key facts: River 92 km long; source at Peña de Hierro, 689 m; NASA's MARTE project simulated a robotic Mars drilling mission here in 2005. Coordinates: Peña del Hierro visitor-center parking (approximate)
Geology and minerals: Jarosite, schwertmannite, goethite, hematite; massive pyrite

Suggested mission tasks: Cold-soak tests; shows how far Earth falls short
Strong matches: Coldest surface on Earth, about -98 °C snow surface
Where it breaks: Lunar shadowed craters stay near -233 °C (40 K), far colder; ice sheet, not regolith
Key facts: About -98 °C seems to be close to the coldest Earth's surface can get; coldest spots in shallow dips near the Dome Argus to Dome Fuji ridge. Coordinates: Dome Argus summit, a reference point near the coldest spots
Sources: Scambos et al. 2018 (https://repository.library.noaa.gov/view/noaa/26979/noaa_26979_DS1.pdf); AGU press release (https://news.agu.org/press-release/coldest-place-on-earth-is-colder-than-scientists-thought/)

Strong matches: Driest non-polar desert; highest UV on Earth; perchlorates as on Mars
Key facts: Mean precipitation mostly below 4 mm/yr in the hyperarid core, 0.15 mm in some spots; studied as a Mars analog since 2003. Coordinates: Yungay (abandoned town), approximate

Strong matches: Only known impact crater in a polar desert; permafrost; cold, dry, dusty, high summer UV
Where it breaks: Liquid water in summer; Earth air and gravity
Geology and minerals: Impact breccia with permafrost; shale, siltstone, gneiss
